name: SFTP
license: Open specification (expired IETF Internet-Draft, never an RFC)
summary: The SSH File Transfer Protocol: binary file-system requests (open, read, write, list, rename) carried inside an encrypted SSH session on port 22. Not FTP, and never finished as an RFC.
intro: SFTP runs as the `sftp` subsystem of an SSH connection. SSH has already authenticated the server by its host key, logged the user in with a password or key, and encrypted the channel; SFTP only adds the file operations. The client sends `SSH_FXP_INIT` with its protocol version and the server answers with the lower of the two versions. From then on every request carries an ID and gets a reply: open a file and get a handle, read or write a range of bytes at an offset, close, list a directory, stat, rename, remove, make or remove directories, follow and create symlinks. A client may keep many requests outstanding at once, limited only by buffering and the SSH channel’s flow control. Commands and data share the one SSH connection, so there is no second port to open.

The name misleads: SFTP has nothing to do with FTP or FTPS, and TCP port 115, registered as “sftp”, belongs to an unrelated Simple File Transfer Protocol. The specification was never finished. The IETF’s Secure Shell working group revised the draft from protocol version 3 (draft-02, October 2001) up to version 6 (draft-13, July 2006), when it expired. OpenSSH’s `sftp` and `sftp-server` implement version 3 and say they won’t support newer drafts, adding features as named extensions instead, such as `posix-rename@openssh.com`. Version 3 is therefore what most servers speak, including managed services such as AWS Transfer Family, and since OpenSSH 9.0 (April 2022) the `scp` command uses SFTP underneath by default.
strengths: One TCP connection on one port (22) for commands and data: easy to firewall and to pass through NAT
Reuses SSH’s encryption, host keys and login methods, including key-based login for unattended jobs
A real remote file-system protocol: random-access reads and writes, attributes, renames and directory operations, not just whole-file copies
Many requests in flight on one connection, with flow control from the SSH channel
limits: No RFC: implementations follow an expired draft, almost always version 3, and add their own extensions for missing features
Quirks are frozen in for compatibility: OpenSSH reverses the arguments of `SSH_FXP_SYMLINK`, and its standard rename differs from POSIX `rename`
Not compatible with FTP clients, servers or FTPS despite the name, so partners must agree which one they mean

Trust rests on SSH host keys: the client must already know the server’s public key, usually from a local list it maintains, and skipping that check on a first connection leaves it open to man-in-the-middle attacks

story: Tatu Ylönen wrote the first version of SSH in spring 1995, at a time when telnet and FTP were widely used, and designed it to replace both. He asked IANA for a port in July 1995 and got 22, between FTP’s 21 and telnet’s 23. When SSH became popular he took it to the IETF, whose Secure Shell working group standardised SSH version 2 as RFCs 4251 to 4254 in January 2006.

File transfer was meant to be part of that suite. In October 2001 Ylönen and Sami Lehtinen of SSH Communications Security published the SSH File Transfer Protocol draft, version 3, describing it as the standard file transfer protocol for SSH2 and usable over any reliable data stream. The working group kept extending it, to version 6 in draft-13 of July 2006, but the draft expired and never became an RFC. OpenSSH had already shipped version 3 and decided not to follow the newer drafts. In April 2022 OpenSSH 9.0 switched `scp` from the old scp/rcp protocol to SFTP by default, because legacy scp expanded remote file names through the remote shell.

choices.choice: A subsystem of SSH, not a protocol of its own on the wire
choices.why: The draft assumes it runs over a secure channel where the server has already authenticated the user, so it needs no encryption or login of its own and inherits everything SSH provides.

choices.choice: File-system operations, not commands and files
choices.why: The draft was designed so it could implement a secure remote file system as well as file transfer: handles, offsets and attributes rather than FTP’s whole-file `RETR` and `STOR`.
Both sides agree on the lower version at start-up, and `SSH_FXP_EXTENDED` lets implementations add named features without a new version, which is how OpenSSH grew it while staying on version 3.

timeline.text: Tatu Ylönen releases SSH 1.0; IANA assigns it port 22
SSH File Transfer Protocol draft-02 defines protocol version 3
SSH-2 published as RFCs 4251 to 4254; SFTP draft-13 (version 6) is the last before it expires
OpenSSH 9.0 makes `scp` use the SFTP protocol by default
